analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to report PFAS 'forever chemical' releases and sets national drinking water limits.
analysis.headline: The bill, a bipartisan Senate compromise on PFAS contamination, cleared the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar in June 2019, but the Senate never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, and firefighting foam that don't break down and have been linked to health problems. This bill would have forced facilities that make or use certain PFAS to publicly report their releases through the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory, required the EPA to set national drinking water standards for PFOA and PFOS, funded nationwide testing of water sources, and let the Pentagon pay to clean up contaminated water near its installations. It passed through the Senate environment committee with bipartisan support but was never brought up for a vote on the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water contaminated with PFAS — including communities near military bases, industrial plants, and airports where firefighting foam was used — would learn what is being released nearby, get enforceable federal drinking water limits for PFOA and PFOS, and benefit from a nationwide survey of PFAS in water sources and federal grants to help water systems, with at least a quarter of that grant money reserved for disadvantaged communities and small systems.

how_it_helps.text: Adds PFOA, PFOS, and related PFAS to the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory with a low 100-pound reporting threshold, so facilities must publicly disclose how much of these chemicals they release [S2] [S3] [S4].
Requires the EPA to set a national drinking water regulation for PFOA and PFOS within two years and to consider regulating additional PFAS [S3] [S4].
Directs the U.S. Geological Survey to sample PFAS concentrations nationwide in drinking water sources, with priority given to sources near known or suspected release sites [S3] [S4].

Authorizes $100 million per year through 2024 in drinking water state revolving fund grants to address PFAS and other emerging contaminants, with at least 25 percent reserved for disadvantaged communities and systems serving fewer than 25,000 people [S4].
Authorizes the Department of Defense to fund cleanup of PFAS-contaminated ground or surface water through agreements with local water authorities and state, local, or tribal governments [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and industrial facilities that make or use PFAS bear new reporting duties, including a retroactive data call covering every PFAS made since 2006, and would eventually face the cost of meeting drinking water standards; public water systems take on monitoring and treatment obligations, though federal grant money and a five-year grace period on penalties soften that load.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS makers and public water systems

drawbacks.text: The bill bars the EPA from imposing any financial penalties for PFAS drinking water violations until five years after a PFAS drinking water regulation is issued, delaying accountability for systems that keep serving contaminated water [S3] [S4].

Monitoring requirements for smaller water systems — those serving between 3,300 and 10,000 people, and a representative sample of smaller systems — apply only 'subject to the availability of appropriations' and can be waived if laboratory capacity is insufficient, so residents served by small systems could be left untested [S4].
The EPA can waive the required PFAS health advisory if it determines a substance is substantially unlikely to occur in drinking water, leaving a judgment call in the agency's discretion [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health payoff — disclosure of where PFAS is released, enforceable drinking water limits, and a nationwide map of contamination — clearly outweighs the compliance costs, which fall mostly on the companies that created the hazard. The main honest criticism is the bill's own compromise design: it delays penalties for five years and makes small-system monitoring conditional on funding, so relief for some communities would have been slow even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it in June 2019 and put it on the Senate's general calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled in the remaining eighteen months of the Congress, so it died there.

narrative.text: Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) introduced the bill on May 16, 2019, joined by Senators Gillibrand and Carper, and it was referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S6].

On June 19, 2019, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, an expanded version that added drinking water standards, nationwide PFAS sampling, and Pentagon cleanup authority to the original disclosure-only bill [S3] [S6].

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 119) on June 19, 2019, and no further action — no floor debate, no vote — ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and facilities that released these chemicals gained the most from the bill's death, because they avoided public release reporting, a retroactive data call, and future drinking water limits; communities living with PFAS contamination got none of the promised disclosure or cleanup help from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PFAS Release Disclosure Act and shepherded it through committee as the lead Republican sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand and Thomas Carper
for.what_they_did: Joined the Republican sponsor at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one.

for.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
for.role: Senate committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY)
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 19, 2019, expanding it into a comprehensive PFAS package, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate floor leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and party leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote in the eighteen months after it was placed on the legislative calendar; the Congress ended without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with two Democratic cosponsors and was reported favorably by the Republican-led committee, so the absence of a floor vote was not a partisan split on the bill itself.

industries.note: The bill would have forced public reporting of PFAS releases, required a data call covering every PFAS made since 2006, and driven drinking water standards that shift cleanup and treatment costs back to the industry. Its interest in avoiding disclosure ran against residents' interest in knowing what is in their water.

Utilities would face new monitoring and eventually treatment obligations, but the bill delays penalties for five years, tailors monitoring for systems consistently below limits, and provides $100 million a year in grants with a quarter reserved for small and disadvantaged communities.

industries.industry: Department of Defense and military installations
industries.note: Military firefighting foam is a major PFAS contamination source near bases, and the bill would have committed Pentagon money to cleaning up affected water, benefiting neighbors of installations while adding cleanup obligations for the Department.

Nationwide USGS sampling, a detection performance standard, expanded drinking water monitoring, and state technical-assistance programs would have generated sustained demand for PFAS testing services.
